items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "diffuse reflection".
items.answer: Reflection from a rough surface in which parallel rays are scattered in many directions, so no image forms
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: reflection from a rough surface in which parallel rays are scattered in many directions, so no image forms. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why angles in reflection are measured from the normal rather than from the mirror surface.
items.answer: The normal is well defined for any surface, including curved ones, so the law of reflection applies everywhere; measuring from the surface would give confusing values on curved mirrors.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The normal is well defined for any surface, including curved ones, so the law of reflection applies everywhere; measuring from the surface would give confusing values on curved mirrors. items.stem: A student claims that the angle of reflection is measured between the ray and the mirror. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Both angles are measured from the normal (at 90° to the mirror).
items.markingKey: Both angles are measured from the normal (at 90° to the mirror). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Leila shone a ray box at a plane mirror and measured the angle of reflection for different angles of incidence, using a protractor.

Angle of incidence / ° | Angle of reflection / °: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
10 | 9 | 9 | 9
20 | 17 | 18 | 17
30 | 27 | 25 | 25
40 | 34 | 34 | 34
50 | 44 | 43 | 43

Calculate the mean angle of reflection when the angle of incidence was 50 °.
items.markingKey: M1 (44 + 43 + 43) ÷ 3; A1 43.3 ° (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Lukas plans an investigation into whether the angle of reflection is always equal to the angle of incidence for a plane mirror. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (angle of incidence (10° to 80° in 10° steps, measured from the normal)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "diffuse reflection"?
options: Reflection from a rough surface in which parallel rays are scattered in many directions, so no image forms
An imaginary line drawn at 90° to a surface at the point where a ray meets it
How high or low a sound seems, determined by its frequency
Reflection from a smooth surface in which parallel rays stay parallel, forming a clear image
items.answer: Reflection from a rough surface in which parallel rays are scattered in many directions, so no image forms
items.markingKey: A. "diffuse reflection" is reflection from a rough surface in which parallel rays are scattered in many directions, so no image forms.

items.stem: "Rough surfaces do not obey the law of reflection." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Each ray still obeys i = r at the point it hits; the normals point in different directions, so rays scatter.
items.markingKey: Each ray still obeys i = r at the point it hits; the normals point in different directions, so rays scatter. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A person stands 4.0 m from a plane mirror and walks 1.0 m towards it. By how much does the distance between the person and their image decrease?
items.answer: 2 m
items.markingKey: 1 new separation = 2 × 3 = 6 m (was 8 m); 1 decrease 2 m.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Apollo lunar laser-ranging retroreflectors shows reflection and timing.
items.answer: Astronauts left corner-cube reflectors on the Moon in 1969; lasers from Earth are reflected straight back, measuring the distance to within a few centimetres. Two or three perpendicular mirrors send light back parallel to its path; distance = speed of light × time ÷ 2.
items.markingKey: Context (Astronauts left corner-cube reflectors on the Moon in 1969; lasers from Earth are reflected straight back, measuring the distance to within a few centimetres.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Two or three perpendicular mirrors send light back parallel to its path; distance = speed of light × time ÷ 2. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to reflection and timing.

items.stem: Two plane mirrors are placed at 90° to each other. A ray hits the first mirror at an angle of incidence of 30°. (a) Calculate the angle of reflection at the first mirror. (b) Calculate the angle of incidence at the second mirror. (c) Show that the ray leaves parallel to its original direction but reversed, and state one use of this arrangement.
items.answer: (a) 30° (b) the reflected ray meets the second mirror at 60° to its normal (90° − 30°) (c) total turn = 180°, so the ray returns parallel; used in bicycle reflectors, cat’s eyes and laser ranging.
items.markingKey: (a) 30° (b) the reflected ray meets the second mirror at 60° to its normal (90° − 30°) (c) total turn = 180°, so the ray returns parallel; used in bicycle reflectors, cat’s eyes and laser ranging.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A thin glass or plastic fibre that carries light along its length by repeated total internal reflection"?
items.answer: optical fibre

items.stem: Briefly explain why light bends towards the normal when it enters glass from air at an angle.
items.answer: Light slows down in glass; the part of the wavefront that enters first slows first, so the wavefront turns and the ray bends towards the normal.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Light slows down in glass; the part of the wavefront that enters first slows first, so the wavefront turns and the ray bends towards the normal. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Rafael writes: "Total internal reflection can happen when light goes from air into water." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It only happens going from a denser to a less dense medium (e.g. water to air).
items.markingKey: It only happens going from a denser to a less dense medium (e.g. water to air). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Lars plans to investigate how the angle of incidence affects the angle of refraction when light enters a glass block, to find the refractive index of the glass. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: the same glass block; colour of light (use one filter); narrow ray from the same ray box; drawing the normal accurately at 90°
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: the same glass block – different blocks have different refractive indices; colour of light (use one filter) – different colours refract by different amounts; narrow ray from the same ray box – wide rays reduce precision; drawing the normal accurately at 90° – angle errors. items.stem:
Noah shone a ray into a semicircular glass block and measured the angle of refraction for different angles of incidence.

Angle of incidence / ° | Angle of refraction / °: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
10 | 6.5 | 6.1 | 6.3
20 | 12.6 | 12.6 | 12.6
30 | 18.1 | 17.7 | 18.8
40 | 24.3 | 24.8 | 23.6
50 | 29.9 | 29.7 | 28.0

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The angle of refraction increases with the angle of incidence but is always smaller; the ratio sin i/sin r is about 1.5. Light slows down in glass and bends towards the normal; Snell’s law gives a constant ratio sin i ÷ sin r equal to the refractive index.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The angle of refraction increases with the angle of incidence but is always smaller; the ratio sin i/sin r is about 1.5.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Light slows down in glass and bends towards the normal; Snell’s law gives a constant ratio sin i ÷ sin r equal to the refractive index.

Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Fibre-optic broadband should be installed in every rural community, paid for by governments."
items.answer: Fibre gives the best long-term service; public funding is justified where markets will not provide it, though other technologies may suit the most remote places.

Arguments against: very expensive to lay cables to remote areas; satellite or 5G may be cheaper alternatives; public money could be spent on other priorities. items.stem: Define the term "refractive index (n)".
items.answer: The ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to its speed in a material: n = c/v; also n = sin i ÷ sin r for light entering from air

items.stem: Explain how optical fibres carry signals around bends.
items.answer: Light hits the inside surface of the fibre at angles greater than the critical angle, so it is totally internally reflected again and again along the fibre with very little loss.

items.stem: Distinguish between angle of incidence and critical angle.
items.answer: The angle of incidence is any angle between the incident ray and the normal; the critical angle is the particular angle of incidence (in the denser medium) that gives a refracted angle of 90°.

items.stem: Using undersea fibre-optic cables linking continents as an example, explain optical fibres.
items.answer: Cables such as MAREA (Spain-USA, 2017) carry over 200 terabits per second using infrared light pulses. Infrared pulses are trapped in the glass core by total internal reflection and travel thousands of kilometres with little loss.
items.markingKey: Context (Cables such as MAREA (Spain-USA, 2017) carry over 200 terabits per second using infrared light pulses.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Outline one way in which endoscopes used in keyhole surgery shows total internal reflection.
items.answer: A bundle of optical fibres carries light into the body and an image back out through a small incision. Light inside each fibre hits the walls above the critical angle and is totally reflected, so it travels along a curved path.
items.markingKey: Context (A bundle of optical fibres carries light into the body and an image back out through a small incision.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: An optical fibre has a glass core of refractive index 1.52. (a) Calculate the critical angle at the core–air boundary. (b) Explain why the fibre is surrounded by a cladding of lower refractive index (1.48) and calculate the new critical angle at the core–cladding boundary using sin c = n₂/n₁. (c) Explain one advantage of optical fibres over copper cables for internet data.
items.answer: (a) sin c = 1/1.52, c = 41.1° (b) cladding protects the core surface from scratches and prevents light leaking into touching fibres; sin c = 1.48/1.52, c = 76.8° (c) higher bandwidth / less signal loss over long distances / no electrical interference.

items.stem: Which type of lens is used to correct short-sightedness?
items.answer: Diverging (concave)

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why a camera must change the distance between the lens and the sensor to focus on near and far objects.
items.answer: The image distance depends on the object distance; for nearer objects the real image forms further behind the lens, so the lens is moved to put the image on the sensor. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.stem: Outline one way in which bats using echolocation shows echoes and ultrasound.
items.answer: Bats emit ultrasound pulses of 20-100 kHz and listen for echoes to locate insects in the dark. The time delay of the echo shows the distance to the insect; short wavelengths give detailed information about small targets.
items.markingKey: Context (Bats emit ultrasound pulses of 20-100 kHz and listen for echoes to locate insects in the dark.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The time delay of the echo shows the distance to the insect; short wavelengths give detailed information about small targets. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to echoes and ultrasound.

items.stem: "Total internal reflection can happen when light goes from air into water." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It only happens going from a denser to a less dense medium (e.g. water to air).
items.markingKey: It only happens going from a denser to a less dense medium (e.g. water to air). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Apollo lunar laser-ranging retroreflectors and explain what it reveals about reflection and timing.
items.answer: Astronauts left corner-cube reflectors on the Moon in 1969; lasers from Earth are reflected straight back, measuring the distance to within a few centimetres. Two or three perpendicular mirrors send light back parallel to its path; distance = speed of light × time ÷ 2.
items.markingKey: Context (Astronauts left corner-cube reflectors on the Moon in 1969; lasers from Earth are reflected straight back, measuring the distance to within a few centimetres.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Two or three perpendicular mirrors send light back parallel to its path; distance = speed of light × time ÷ 2. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to reflection and timing.

items.stem: Lukas wants to find out how the object distance affects the image distance for a converging lens, in order to find its focal length. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does object distance u from the lens affect image distance v?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (object distance u from the lens (20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 60 cm)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (image distance v – distance from lens to screen when the image is sharpest, measured with a metre rule) in a question form.

items.stem: With reference to sonar mapping of the ocean floor, explain how it illustrates echo-sounding.
items.answer: Ships send sound pulses downward and time the echoes to map the sea bed, e.g. the search for flight MH370 in the Indian Ocean. Depth = speed of sound in water × time ÷ 2.
items.markingKey: Context (Ships send sound pulses downward and time the echoes to map the sea bed, e.g. the search for flight MH370 in the Indian Ocean.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: depth = speed of sound in water × time ÷ 2. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to echo-sounding.

items.stem: Describe how you would use a semicircular glass block and a ray box to measure the critical angle of glass, and use your result to calculate the refractive index. Include one source of uncertainty and how to reduce it.
items.answer: Aim the ray at the centre of the flat face from inside the curved side (so it enters the curved face along a normal); increase the angle until the refracted ray just runs along the flat face (90°); mark and measure the angle of incidence = critical angle (≈ 42°); n = 1/sin c ≈ 1.5. Uncertainty: judging the exact angle where refraction stops – repeat, approach from both sides, use a narrow ray in a dark room.
items.markingKey: Aim the ray at the centre of the flat face from inside the curved side (so it enters the curved face along a normal); increase the angle until the refracted ray just runs along the flat face (90°); mark and measure the angle of incidence = critical angle (≈ 42°); n = 1/sin c ≈ 1.5. Uncertainty: judging the exact angle where refraction stops – repeat, approach from both sides, use a narrow ray in a dark room.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that mirrors on roads and in shops (convex safety mirrors) should be used more widely instead of cameras.
items.answer: Mirrors are a cheap safety aid at junctions; cameras serve different purposes such as recording.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: no power needed, cheap and reliable; show a wide field of view to drivers at blind junctions. Arguments against: images are small and distances are hard to judge; cameras can record evidence and be monitored remotely. Supported judgement: Mirrors are a cheap safety aid at junctions; cameras serve different purposes such as recording. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: "Laser eye surgery is a better solution than glasses for short-sightedness." Discuss.
items.answer: It is a good option for suitable adults, but glasses remain safer, cheaper and reversible for many people.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: permanent correction, no glasses or contacts; convenient for sport and work. Arguments against: expensive and not available everywhere; small risk of complications (dry eyes, glare); not suitable for everyone; vision can still change with age. Supported judgement: It is a good option for suitable adults, but glasses remain safer, cheaper and reversible for many people. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Kwame plans an investigation into how the temperature of air affects the speed of sound. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (air temperature (°C), changed by testing in a warm room, outdoors and in a cold store) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Which equation is Snell’s law (light entering from air)?
items.answer: n = sin i ÷ sin r
items.markingKey: A. Ratio of sines.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "normal"?
options: How high or low a sound seems, determined by its frequency
An imaginary line drawn at 90° to a surface at the point where a ray meets it
Reflection from a rough surface in which parallel rays are scattered in many directions, so no image forms
Sound with a frequency above 20 000 Hz, beyond the range of human hearing
items.answer: An imaginary line drawn at 90° to a surface at the point where a ray meets it
items.markingKey: B. "normal" is an imaginary line drawn at 90° to a surface at the point where a ray meets it.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "principal focus (focal point)"?
options: How loud a sound seems, determined by its amplitude
Sound with a frequency above 20 000 Hz, beyond the range of human hearing
The point where rays parallel to the principal axis meet (or appear to come from) after passing through a lens
The ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to its speed in a material: n = c/v; also n = sin i ÷ sin r for light entering from air
items.answer: The point where rays parallel to the principal axis meet (or appear to come from) after passing through a lens
items.markingKey: C. "principal focus (focal point)" is the point where rays parallel to the principal axis meet (or appear to come from) after passing through a lens.

items.stem: Explain the difference between pitch and loudness.
items.answer: Pitch depends on frequency (higher frequency → higher note); loudness depends on amplitude (larger amplitude → louder).
items.markingKey: Pitch depends on frequency (higher frequency → higher note); loudness depends on amplitude (larger amplitude → louder). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that total internal reflection can happen when light goes from air into water. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It only happens going from a denser to a less dense medium (e.g. water to air).
items.markingKey: It only happens going from a denser to a less dense medium (e.g. water to air). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between specular reflection and diffuse reflection.
items.answer: Specular reflection from a smooth surface keeps parallel rays parallel and forms an image; diffuse reflection from a rough surface scatters rays in many directions.
items.markingKey: Specular reflection from a smooth surface keeps parallel rays parallel and forms an image; diffuse reflection from a rough surface scatters rays in many directions. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "All images formed by converging lenses are upright." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Real images from converging lenses are inverted; only the virtual image (object inside the focal length) is upright.
items.markingKey: Real images from converging lenses are inverted; only the virtual image (object inside the focal length) is upright. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Jonas writes: "A higher-pitched sound travels faster through air." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: All frequencies travel at the same speed in air; higher pitch means higher frequency and shorter wavelength.
items.markingKey: All frequencies travel at the same speed in air; higher pitch means higher frequency and shorter wavelength. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why a swimming pool appears shallower than it really is.
items.answer: Light from the bottom refracts away from the normal as it leaves the water; the eye traces the rays back in straight lines, so they appear to come from a point higher than the real bottom.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Light from the bottom refracts away from the normal as it leaves the water; the eye traces the rays back in straight lines, so they appear to come from a point higher than the real bottom. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Zara writes: "The angle of reflection is measured between the ray and the mirror." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Both angles are measured from the normal (at 90° to the mirror).
items.markingKey: Both angles are measured from the normal (at 90° to the mirror). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Sofia placed a candle at different distances from a converging lens and moved a screen until the image was sharp, measuring the image distance.

Object distance / cm | Image distance / cm: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
20 | 58.3 | 58.1 | 59.7
25 | 24.6 | 38.1 | 38.2
30 | 30.0 | 29.6 | 30.6
40 | 24.6 | 23.7 | 23.0
60 | 20.5 | 19.8 | 19.5

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean image distance at 25 cm, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 24.6 cm (trial 1 at 25 cm); mean = 38.15 cm

items.stem: In an investigation into how the angle of incidence affects the angle of refraction when light enters a glass block, to find the refractive index of the glass, state the dependent variable and describe how Mateo should measure it.
items.answer: angle of refraction in the glass, found by marking the ray path and measuring with a protractor
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: angle of refraction in the glass, found by marking the ray path and measuring with a protractor.

items.stem: Outline one way in which periscopes used in submarines and in crowds shows the law of reflection.
items.answer: Two plane mirrors at 45° let the user see over obstacles. Each mirror turns the light through 90° because i = r = 45°, so light from above reaches the eye.
items.markingKey: Context (Two plane mirrors at 45° let the user see over obstacles.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Each mirror turns the light through 90° because i = r = 45°, so light from above reaches the eye. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the law of reflection.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Hubble Space Telescope mirror problem (1990) and its fix (1993) and explain what it reveals about focusing and correction of images.
items.answer: Hubble’s main mirror was ground to the wrong shape, producing blurry images; astronauts installed corrective optics like “glasses”. Additional optics changed the paths of the light rays so they came to a sharp focus, just as lenses correct eyesight.
items.markingKey: Context (Hubble’s main mirror was ground to the wrong shape, producing blurry images; astronauts installed corrective optics like “glasses”.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Additional optics changed the paths of the light rays so they came to a sharp focus, just as lenses correct eyesight. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to focusing and correction of images.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that fibre-optic broadband should be installed in every rural community, paid for by governments.
items.answer: Fibre gives the best long-term service; public funding is justified where markets will not provide it, though other technologies may suit the most remote places.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: much faster, more reliable internet for education, healthcare and business; reduces the digital divide. Arguments against: very expensive to lay cables to remote areas; satellite or 5G may be cheaper alternatives; public money could be spent on other priorities. Supported judgement: Fibre gives the best long-term service; public funding is justified where markets will not provide it, though other technologies may suit the most remote places.

items.stem: A fishing boat’s sonar sends a pulse and receives two echoes: one after 0.020 s from a shoal of fish and one after 0.12 s from the sea bed. The speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m/s. (a) Calculate the depth of the fish and of the sea bed. (b) Explain why sonar uses ultrasound rather than audible sound. (c) Discuss one environmental concern about high-intensity sonar.
items.answer: (a) fish 1500 × 0.020 ÷ 2 = 15 m; sea bed 1500 × 0.12 ÷ 2 = 90 m. (b) Short wavelength gives detailed images of small objects and the beam can be directed; does not disturb people. (c) Powerful military sonar has been linked to whale and dolphin strandings because it interferes with their echolocation and hearing.
